text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementGeoscienceISS Astronaut Spots Moon-like Mountains From SpaceEarth and the moon have a shared geological historyDNBy David Nield3:00 PM CDT on October 14, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleThere may be a couple of hundred thousand miles between Earth and the moon, but our planet shares some striking geological similarities with our nearest neighbor in the sky. One of those similarities is the rock anorthosite.Powered By 10 ShareNextStayThe crystalline rock makes up much of the lunar highlands—it’s the lighter colored gray you can see when you look up at the moon—and its core mineral is the most common on the lunar surface. It’s thought to have formed during the initial cooling of the moon, as magma hardened into solid rock after its violent birth.On Earth, you can also find anorthosite across several continents, though it’s less widespread than it is on the moon.
